papers.title: The American Medical Directory Panel: Comparing AI-Assisted and LLM Transcription with Manual Data Entry at Scale
papers.abstract: How closely does machine transcription agree with manual double-entry data? We digitize the 1912 and 1921 editions of the American Medical Directory, a national register of US physicians with roughly 140,000 and 150,000 entries in the two volumes, and compare five machine-extraction workflows with a full-count double-entered manual transcription. Like many historical directories, the AMD is semi-structured rather than tabular, so errors arise from misreading the layout as well as the text. A script that parses commercial OCR text using rules written by coding agents recovers about 97 percent of manually transcribed records with similar precision, more than a multimodal language model workflow (gemini-2.0.flash) that reads the page images and the OCR text. When the two methods fail, they fail on partly overlapping sets of records, so reconciling their outputs raises both recall and precision to about 98 percent. An open-weight LLM pipeline run on a local GPU server falls between the parser and the multimodal workflow in recall, and replacing the commercial OCR model with an open-source alternative lowers its recall by only about 2 percentage points. As the manual transcription's own error rate is unknown, these rates measure agreement rather than accuracy. Direct processing charges for the commercial OCR and multimodal workflow were about 0.03 euro per page, compared with 14.70 euro per page for manual transcription.

papers.title: Persistence and Change in National Production Networks
papers.abstract: Many country-years in multi-country input-output databases have no national table. We study the kernel of domestic intermediate transactions, the part that rescaling to new industry totals cannot update. Among 25 economies with a national table every year, the latest table misplaces 6.6 percent of the kernel one year ahead and 21.2 percent ten years ahead, while the five most similar economies misplace 24.1 to 25.0 percent at every horizon. In the OECD tables, 88 percent of country-years without a national table lie close to one cross-country template, against 3.6 percent of country-years with a table. The template spreads from 29 economies in 2019 to 67 in 2022. In this sample an own table's error meets its distance to that year's template near fifteen years, not as a general shelf life.

papers.title: Globally promoting legumes by production or use subsidies
papers.abstract: Despite consensus on the positive economic, environmental, and health effects of expanding legume production and consumption, the share of cropland devoted to them remains relatively small, and their share of human consumption is negligible compared with other protein sources such as meat. The presence of externalities associated with legume production and consumption gives room for policy interventions. In this context, we estimate the effects of global subsidies on legume production and consumption using CGEBox, an open-source and open-access Computable General Equilibrium modelling platform, with integrated accounting for land use, land cover, and energy, and considering agricultural and non-agricultural households. The analysis offers high agri-food detail and a special focus on Ghana and Germany, two countries with different agroecological and socioeconomic conditions facing multiple food system issues. Compared to production subsidies, we find that use subsidies are more effective at reducing consumer prices of legumes and stimulating household intake of macronutrients, without displacing consumption of other foods. In contrast, production subsidies are more effective at boosting domestic supply, but also stimulate their feed use. Furthermore, subsidies drive up crop land to the detriment of pasture land and forests. The impact of these subsidies also reveals profound regional disparities, influenced by patterns of land use and of production and consumption.

papers.title: Structural economic change under the digital transformation
papers.abstract: Productivity improvements in digital industries could massively reshape the structure of production networks and drive significant labour reallocation across sectors. We examine these adjustments using a calibrated agent-based model of the global economy. We consider two scenarios with the same cumulative increase in digital-supplier productivity, which differ in how digital inputs in exposed industries are incorporated into production. The key difference is whether digital inputs enter as standard intermediate inputs (low embeddedness) or are combined directly with primary factors (high embeddedness). Across economies, both scenarios generate gains in gross output, household utility, and GDP, although value-added gains are more modest and unevenly distributed across sectors. High embeddedness generally amplifies production responses, particularly in industries highly exposed to digital inputs. Structurally, as digital industries become central in the production network and attract labour from other activities, other industries move further upstream and downstream. Persistent labour reallocation pressures also indicate potential unemployment risks where workers cannot move to expanding industries. These findings stress that, beyond productivity gains derived from advances in digital technologies, economic and social consequences depend on how digital inputs integrate into production and on workers' possibilities to adapt to structural change.

papers.title: Equity and Aggregate Ambiguity
papers.abstract: Equitable resource allocations in the context of symmetric risk exposures are intuitively desirable and sometimes even expected in public planning. However, public planners generally are also concerned with mitigating risk and, more generally, uncertainty and ambiguity. We study a fundamental conflict between equity and ambiguity avoidance in public risk allocation problems. Our main results are framed and established in the setting of general symmetric aggregate losses equipped with dependence uncertainty among individual losses. Specializing to the classical model of Keeney (1980), we prove that an increase in equity is equivalent to an increase in aggregate ambiguity. We then provide a quantitative characterization of equity and ambiguity avoidance through the $\alpha$-maxmin preference framework, establishing conditions on ambiguity and risk attitudes under which each criterion holds. Specifically, equity corresponds to ambiguity or risk proneness, while ambiguity avoidance corresponds to ambiguity or risk aversion. The analysis extends to general classes of symmetric aggregation functions, where we show that ambiguity attitude is the primary determinant of preference, though aggregation structure and risk attitude also play important roles. Numerical illustrations validate our theoretical findings and explore the equity-ambiguity tradeoff.

papers.title: Interpreting the Morbidity Gap
papers.abstract: The Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study now reports the morbidity gap (MG), life expectancy minus healthy life expectancy, as an indicator in its own right. Writing MG as the expected cumulative rate of years lived with disability (YLDs) at the life-table age at death, we use stochastic dominance results to show what MG measures, how it responds to mortality and how it relates to the YLDs of the current population. We show the following. (a) A YLD profile gives an MG no larger than another's under every life table if and only if its cumulative YLD rate is nowhere higher. (b) With YLD rates fixed, lower mortality at every age widens MG, so that removing a risk factor that raises mortality reduces MG by less than its contribution to MG in GBD's risk factor attribution. (c) A family of results gives easily interpretable conditions on the age structure of the population for the crude YLD rate to be above or below the life-table YLD rate, which is MG divided by life expectancy, and these conditions change with population ageing. We illustrate the results for Singapore, where MG widened from 8.9 to 11.2 years between 1990 and 2023.

papers.title: Incomplete-market CAPM equilibria in continuous time
papers.abstract: We study continuous-time CAPM equilibria with general mean-variance preferences of the form $U(\mu,\sigma)$, where $U$ is strictly quasiconcave, increasing in the mean $\mu$ and decreasing in the volatility $\sigma$ of terminal wealth. Our framework accommodates both financial and productive assets with nontradeable endowments. We allow for equilibria driven by general semimartingales in the case of linear mean-variance preferences and by continuous semimartingales in the case of general mean-variance preferences. The key insight is a connection between mean-variance efficiency and quadratic utility maximisation. We first characterise quadratic equilibria through an explicit family of equilibrium price processes indexed by the aggregate risk tolerance. We then show that each agent's optimal mean-variance strategy corresponds to a quadratic optimum with an endogenously determined risk tolerance. This correspondence reduces the mean-variance equilibrium problem to a one-dimensional fixed-point problem, whose solvability we establish using fine properties of (dynamic) mean-variance hedging and a novel stability result for quadratic BSDEs with BMO growth at the origin. Finally, examples illustrate how unspanned stochastic-volatility risk interacts with aggregate endowments to affect equilibrium asset prices, and how nonlinear mean-variance preferences influence equilibrium risk tolerance and asset-price comparative statics.

papers.title: Multiscale Reconstruction of Weighted Networks from Coarse-Grained Data
papers.abstract: Network reconstruction from partial information is usually performed at the same resolution level at which constraints are observable. This becomes problematic when only coarse-grained information is available, while the relevant process occurs at a finer scale. Here we employ the multiscale model of weighted networks introduced in a companion paper and turn it into a probabilistic framework for reconstructing weighted networks across arbitrary aggregation levels. The model is built to preserve its functional form under coarse-graining, so that global parameters calibrated on an observable aggregate layer can be transferred to finer layers without refitting. We test the method on two empirical systems with different aggregation mechanisms. In the International Trade Network, countries are aggregated into geographic macro-regions and the observed coarse-grained layer is used to infer the underlying country-level network. In the Dutch production network, sectoral flows are reconstructed across the hierarchical industrial classification, using coarser sectoral layers to infer finer ones. In both geographical and sectoral settings, we benchmark our genuinely multiscale reconstruction method against a state-of-the-art weighted reconstruction model calibrated directly at the target resolution, and therefore using additional information available at the same (finer) scale at which performance is evaluated. Despite this informational disadvantage, our method recovers the fine-scale binary structure with high accuracy, improving precision, specificity, accuracy and maximum degree-error diagnostics, while remaining nearly equivalent in sensitivity.

papers.title: Firm Entry and Exit with Unbounded Productivity
papers.abstract: In Hopenhayn's (1992) entry-exit model productivity is bounded, implying that the predicted firm size distribution cannot match the power law tail observable in the data. In this paper we remove the boundedness assumption and, in this more general setting, provide an exact characterization of existence of stationary equilibria, as well as a novel sufficient condition for existence based on treating production as a Lyapunov function. We also provide new representations of the rate of entry and aggregate supply. Market clearing rules out stationary competitive equilibria at or below Zipf's law. Under monopolistic competition where the demand for each firm's variety bounds its sales, a stationary equilibrium exists for every tail index of productivity. In an example with additive preferences, unbounded markups inherit the Pareto tail of productivity.

papers.title: Shared Models, Selective Trading, and Order Flow
papers.abstract: We study whether the diversity of language models installed in a trading population carries over to the orders that reach the market. In simulated markets with five agents from each of three open-weight model families, we change only how a corporate announcement is presented and estimate each family's share of active orders. In two matched experiments, explanatory layoff text multiplies Mistral's participation by 5.3 (from 14.0% to 74.7% of opportunities) and raises its share of announcement-round orders from 17.5% to 57.4%. In a preregistered study of six new events, adding one favorable and one unfavorable evaluation to identical facts changes active composition in a main sample and in an independently worded replication (average e-values of 6.3x10^25 and 6.7x10^40, against a threshold of 20). Within an event, the change reallocates on average 21% of active decisions across families in the main sample and 14% in the replication. The same reallocation appears under both wordings in three of the six events; in the other three, the families that gain differ. Evaluative text also lowers every family's average participation and lowers executed net flow in all twelve event-sample cells, and family contributions mostly reinforce one another. In the financing event of the first study, active composition changed substantially while net flow barely moved, because family responses offset one another. In a stylized market-clearing benchmark, price accuracy depends on both the number and the composition of active traders. The experiments do not identify why the models respond to evaluations, and they do not estimate effects on price accuracy.
